question.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=2x+3.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+3|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+3|+C & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+3|+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+3|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|2x+3|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|2x+3|).
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=3x+3.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{6}{3x+3}\,\text{d}x & =6\int \frac{1}{3x+3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+3|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=2\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+3|+C & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+3|+2\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+3|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|3x+3|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{6}{3x+3}\,\text{d}x=2\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|3x+3|).
$$

generation.domain: x real excluding -1; K>0; C arbitrary real on each connected interval

question.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{2}{5-3x}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=5-3x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{5-3x}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{5-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-3x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-3x|+C & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-3x|-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-3x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5-3x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{2}{5-3x}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5-3x|).
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{9-5x}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=9-5x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{9-5x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|9-5x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|9-5x|+C & =-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|9-5x|-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|9-5x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|9-5x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{9-5x}\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|9-5x|).
$$
